citations.quote: If $X$ has finitely many cells and $c_n(X)$ is its number of $n$-cells, define $\chi(X)=\sum_n(-1)^nc_n(X)$. The sum is finite by hypothesis.

derivations.claim: **Trivialize a finite cover over a single cell without a choice axiom.** Away from the branch values the stated proper local models give a finite covering. For completeness, properness and a finite fiber give an evenly covered neighborhood: choose disjoint local inverse neighborhoods about the finitely many preimages, shrink their common image, and exclude any further preimages by compactness. A covering over an interval or an open triangle is trivial. Indeed, lift a path from a fixed point and a specified preimage by subdividing its compact parameter interval into finitely many pieces mapped into evenly covered neighborhoods; on each piece the preceding endpoint selects the unique sheet. Uniqueness on overlapping pieces makes refinement irrelevant. For a homotopy of paths, compactness of the parameter square gives a finite rectangular grid whose image on each small rectangle lies in one evenly covered neighborhood. Starting along the initial edge and using its chosen sheet on each rectangle proves by induction that endpoint-fixed homotopic paths lift to the same endpoint. Every loop in an interval or triangle contracts by straight-line interpolation. Hence, for each of the finitely many points in a single fiber, lifting paths defines a unique section over the cell, independent of the path. It is continuous because in a small evenly covered neighborhood it is the inverse of a single sheet. These finitely many disjoint sections exhaust the cover. This proves that each open edge and face has exactly $d$ homeomorphic lifts; it also proves the same assertion for a closed triangle with its sole possible branch vertex removed, by the straight-line contraction of a triangle with one vertex deleted. All choices here are finite for each particular path or homotopy; path independence defines the section uniquely, with no choice of paths as a family.

**Close the lifted cells and count the deficit at vertices.** At a branch vertex use the specified local sector of $z\mapsto z^{r_x}$. Each inverse sheet on the punctured target sector has a continuous extension to its vertex, because $|z|=|w|^{1/r_x}\to0$; an unramified vertex extends by its local inverse. Thus the lifted open cells close to finite topological cells. The sector and at-most-one-branch-vertex hypotheses ensure their attaching maps have precisely the usual cyclic links at interior vertices and interval links at boundary vertices. They give a cellulation of $T$: local inverses cover all nonvertex points, and the local models cover every sector at a vertex. If the target counts are $V,E,F_2$, the lifted edge and face counts are $dE,dF_2$ by step 1.1. At a target vertex $y$, the local degree formula is $\sum_{x\in p^{-1}(y)}r_x=d$, since a nearby regular value has exactly $r_x$ preimages in the local disk about $x$ and no others after shrinking, by properness. Boundary vertices have $d$ unramified preimages. Thus the total vertex count is $dV-\sum_x(r_x-1)$. Substitution in [F1] proves $\chi(T)=d\chi(F)-\sum_x(r_x-1)$. This also applies component by component and to a disk, whose finite cell count is one.

**Cut-piece Euler bookkeeping.** Subdivide the finite graph and the finitely many piece cellulations along the prescribed vertices; the pieces are to be glued along full boundary edges. Inserting a vertex in an edge adds one vertex and one edge and preserves [F1]. Splitting a disk face by an interior edge adds one edge and one face, and inserting a face vertex with $k$ radiating edges adds one vertex, $k$ edges and $k-1$ faces, also preserving the count. The stipulated finite subdivisions therefore retain the lifted counts of step 2.1. The union of all piece interiors with the graph therefore has $\chi(S)=V_H-E_H+\sum_a\chi(P_a)$. To verify this directly from cells, retain all graph vertices and edges only once. For each piece its interior cells contribute $\chi(P_a)-\chi(\partial P_a)$. Every boundary component is a subdivided circle with equal numbers of vertices and edges, so $\chi(\partial P_a)=0$. This proves the formula even when several boundary edges or vertices of one piece are identified in $S$. The boundary preimage and angle hypotheses, and step 2.1 applied to every piece cover, also give $e(D)=\sum_a\chi(P_a)+R_{\mathrm{face}}-\sum_{\text{corner occurrences}}(1/2-\alpha/(2\pi))$. Extra smooth corners have angle $\pi$ and contribute zero, so none is counted twice or lost by subdivision.

**Local link count, including the boundary factor one half.** Let $s_v$ be the number of incident cut-piece corner occurrences at $v$ and $d_v$ its graph valence, counting a loop edge twice. The circular link of an interior vertex has one sector between consecutive edge germs, so $s_v=d_v$. The interval link at a boundary vertex has two endpoint germs along the boundary and all other germs between them, so $s_v=d_v-1$. Also $\sum_v d_v=2E_H$. The corner sum in step 3.1 is $\sum_v(s_v/2-A_v/(2\pi))$. Substitute its expression and the graph Euler formula there to obtain $e(D)=\chi(S)+R_{\mathrm{face}}+\sum_v(d_v/2-1-s_v/2+A_v/(2\pi))$. At an interior vertex this summand is $A_v/(2\pi)-1$; at a boundary vertex it is $A_v/(2\pi)-1/2$. This is the asserted general formula, using only the finite graph link identities. In particular a boundary critical point has not been treated as a full interior branch point.

**Ramification and right-corner specialization.** For an interior vertex with $A_v=2\pi r_v$, the term in step 4.1 is $r_v-1$. At an ordinary boundary vertex with $A_v=\pi r_v$, it is $(r_v-1)/2$. A corner of angle $\pi/2$ has term $-1/4$, and one of angle $3\pi/2$ has term $+1/4$. Separating these four finite sums in step 4.1 gives $e(D)=\chi(S)-c_{90}/4+c_{270}/4+R_{\mathrm{int}}+R_{\mathrm{bdry}}/2$, which rearranges to the claimed formula. The target right-corner expression follows from exactly the same substitution in its defining finite corner sum. This conclusion uses the prescribed angle data, not an unproved assertion that a given analytic or Whitney representative supplies them.

boundaries.evidence: Statement permits empty finite sector sums; in the empty S case the Euler and sector cell counts are all zero. The positive-degree covering assertion concerns nonempty target regions.
Statement and proof: Statement allows zero ramification and no marked corners, with the finite Euler count unchanged.
Statement and proof: Statement includes degree one and a disk of Euler count one; a 90degree corner contributes negative one quarter.
Statement and proof: Statement requires local branched-cover models, explicit adapted finite triangulations and circle/interval graph links; arbitrary Whitney representativity is explicitly excluded.
Statement and proof: The general sector formula has boundary factor one half, with 90/270degree corners handled separately.
Statement and proof: All choices in the proof are finite or uniquely defined by finite path lifting; no choice principle is assumed.
